1592570689078595 | Sep 7, 2026 | Kira Marlo | I packed an overnight bag for my son and told him we were “having an adventure,” not that we didn’t have anywhere else to sleep that night. He was eight. He threw his dinosaur pajamas into the bag, grabbed the stuffed dog he’d slept with since preschool, and asked if we could get snacks for the car. I said yes. That was easier than explaining why there were already three trash bags full of our clothes in the trunk. My name is Danielle Morris. I was thirty-seven years old, working shipping and receiving at a distribution center outside Kansas City, and I’d spent most of the previous month convincing myself everything was about to work out. It didn’t. My car had finally died for good on a Tuesday. The apartment I thought we were moving into fell through Thursday morning. By Thursday night, my son Caleb and I had nowhere that was actually ours to sleep. My sister offered us her guest room. I told Caleb we were staying there for a few nights because it would be fun. “Adventure time,” I called it. He loved that. The first night he jumped onto the guest bed with his stuffed dog and asked if we could eat popcorn while watching a movie. I smiled and said sure. After he fell asleep, I sat on the floor beside the bed searching apartment listings on my phone. Deposit. First month. Application fee. Utility deposit. Another application fee. Every number seemed reasonable by itself. Together, they might as well have been written in another language. I had 217 in checking. Payday was eight days away. My sister never made me feel unwelcome. That almost made it harder. She had two kids of her own, one bathroom, and a husband who woke up at five every morning. Our bags were stacked against the guest-room wall. Caleb’s backpack hung from a dining chair. My work boots lived beside their front door because there wasn’t anywhere else to put them. Every morning, I left for the warehouse in a yellow safety vest. Every afternoon, I picked Caleb up. Every evening, we went back to somebody else’s house. He thought it was temporary. So did I. The first week, I kept everything packed. I didn’t unpack the trash bags. Didn’t put clothes in drawers. Didn’t move our toothbrushes out of the little travel pouch. Temporary people shouldn’t spread out. That was what I told myself. Caleb kept calling it adventure time. “Are we doing adventure time again tonight?” “Yep.” “Can we sleep on the couch Friday?” “We’ll see.” He never asked the question I was afraid of. When are we going home? Maybe that meant he didn’t understand. Or maybe he understood enough not to ask. I was making 20.40 an hour at the distribution center. There was overtime when volume was high, but overtime wasn’t guaranteed. Before everything fell apart, I had been able to keep up. Barely. Then the car started overheating. Then I missed two shifts dealing with it. Then the landlord on the new apartment wanted a larger deposit after running my credit. The numbers stopped cooperating. For the first three weeks at my sister’s, I took every extra hour they offered. If somebody didn’t want a Saturday, I took it. If they needed somebody to stay until nine, I stayed. Caleb spent more time with my sister than he did with me. I told myself it was temporary too. There was a woman I used to see almost every morning at the bus stop near the warehouse. Her name was Renee. We didn’t work together. She worked at a commercial laundry company a few blocks away and took the same early bus I did after my car died. She was maybe forty-five, always wore purple scrubs under a winter coat, and usually looked as tired as I felt. At first our conversations were nothing. Weather. Bus running late. Somebody smoking too close to the shelter. Then I started noticing little things. Renee used to count change before getting on the bus. One morning she tapped her phone instead. A couple weeks later, she wasn’t at the bus stop. Then I saw her pull into the convenience store across the street in a used gray SUV. Not new. Not fancy. But running. I waved when she got out. “You got a car?” “Finally.” “Thought you said your credit was terrible.” “It is.” She smiled like there was more to the answer. A week later, I saw her carrying a grocery bag into work instead of the crackers she usually bought from the vending machine. Then she mentioned taking her granddaughter to the zoo. On a Saturday. That got my attention. Renee worked Saturdays whenever she could. I asked her about it Monday morning. “You stopped taking overtime?” “Some of it.” “Since when?” She shrugged. “Since I didn’t need every single hour anymore.” I looked at her. “What changed?” She hesitated for a second, then pulled out her phone. She sent me a link. “What is this?” “Just watch it.” “To what?” “A video somebody sent me.” “What’s it about?” She shook her head. “I’m not explaining it.” That annoyed me. “Why?” “Because I almost ignored it when somebody tried explaining it to me.” Then her bus came. That was all I got. I didn’t watch it that night. Caleb wanted to build a blanket fort in my sister’s living room. Adventure time. So we did. After everybody went to bed, I folded the blankets, packed his dinosaur pajamas back into the overnight bag, and sat at the kitchen table. The bag was starting to bother me. Sixteen days. Same bag. Still packed. I opened Renee’s message. Watched a few minutes. Closed it. I assumed I knew where it was going. Then I looked across the kitchen at Caleb’s backpack hanging from somebody else’s chair. I opened the video again. I’m not going to tell you what was in it. Renee wouldn’t explain it to me either. Now I understand why. I watched the whole thing. I wasn’t convinced. I didn’t suddenly think I’d found the answer to everything. I mostly thought, “That sounds strange.” The next morning, I watched part of it again while drinking coffee before anyone else woke up. Then I did what it showed me. Nothing dramatic happened. That first week, the first small result covered my bus pass and Caleb’s school lunch account. I didn’t tell anybody. The next one covered the application fee on an apartment I’d been afraid to apply for because I couldn’t afford to lose another fee. I applied. Got denied. That hurt. But for once, the rejection didn’t also cost me grocery money. I kept going. The following week, there was enough for a rental car for two days so I could look at apartments after work without dragging Caleb onto three buses. Then enough to put toward another deposit. Small things. Boring things. Exactly what I needed. I still worked. Still wore the yellow vest. Still took overtime. Still slept in my sister’s guest room. But something started changing. I stopped feeling like every setback sent me back to zero. That mattered. By week four, I had enough put aside that I could turn down a Saturday shift. I almost didn’t. Caleb had asked if we could go to the park. My supervisor said, “You want the overtime or not?” Normally the answer was automatic. “Yes.” This time I said, “Not Saturday.” Caleb and I spent two hours at the park. He brought the stuffed dog. I told him stuffed dogs weren’t supposed to go down slides. He disagreed. That night he said, “Adventure time was good today.” I laughed. Then I went into the bathroom and cried quietly for about a minute. Not because anything was wrong. Because I realized he thought adventure time meant I was around. The next apartment I applied for wasn’t nice. Two bedrooms. Old carpet. Laundry room down the hall. Kitchen cabinet that didn’t close properly. I wanted it immediately. The manager called me at work. Approved. I made her repeat it. Then I walked into the employee restroom and sat on the closed toilet lid staring at the wall. I had enough for the deposit. Not because one huge thing happened. Because enough smaller things had finally stopped going wrong at the same time. We moved in a little over six weeks after we first went to my sister’s. There wasn’t much to move. Trash bags. Two plastic bins. Caleb’s backpack. The overnight bag. My sister gave us an old kitchen table. Renee helped me find a secondhand couch from somebody she knew. The first night, Caleb ran from room to room like the place was enormous. Then he came into the bedroom carrying his dinosaur pajamas. “Are we still doing adventure time?” I looked at him. “What do you mean?” “Do I use the bag?” I hadn’t realized it was still packed. Same toothbrush pouch. Same pajamas. Same stuffed dog tucked under one strap. I emptied it onto the bed. “No. You’ve got drawers now.” He looked disappointed for about three seconds. Then he started putting socks away. That night, after he fell asleep, I sat on the living-room floor. No couch yet. No curtains. One lamp from my sister. But the backpack was hanging on our chair. Our toothbrushes were in our bathroom. My work boots were beside our door. I didn’t have to pack anything before morning. That was the part that got me. A couple months later, the warehouse offered another stretch of Saturday overtime. I took one. Turned down two. Not because I suddenly hated working. Because overtime had stopped being the thing standing between us and disaster. There’s a difference. Renee asked me about it one morning. “You still watching that thing?” “I watched it.” “And?” “I hate that you were right.” She laughed. “I never said I was right.” “You didn’t say anything.” “Exactly.” Then she got into her SUV and drove to work. I eventually replaced my car too. Used. High mileage. The radio only worked when it felt like it. I loved it. The first Friday I picked Caleb up in it, he threw his backpack into the back seat. Then he looked at the overnight bag I’d left in the trunk. “You still have that?” “Yeah.” “Why?” I didn’t know what to say. So I said the first true thing that came to mind. “I guess I forgot to unpack it.” He accepted that. Kids accept a lot of explanations adults spend months arguing with themselves about. I still have that bag. It’s in the top of my closet now. Empty. Sometimes I see it when I’m putting something away. For six weeks, that bag held everything I was willing to admit we needed. Pajamas. Toothbrushes. A stuffed dog. A couple shirts. I called it adventure time because I didn’t know how to tell my son that I couldn’t promise where we would be sleeping a month from then. He made it easier on me by believing the story. Or pretending to. I’m still not sure which. I know what changed after Renee sent me that video. I’m not going to try to explain what was in it. She wouldn’t explain it to me either. Watch it yourself. Maybe you’ll close it after a few minutes. I almost did. Maybe you’ll think it sounds strange. I did. Or maybe you’ll come back to it the next morning and try what it shows you. That’s what I did. Caleb doesn’t call it adventure time anymore. Now when he packs that overnight bag, it means he’s going to stay at my sister’s because he wants to. I like that version better. | go.makemoredaily.com
2223396985107959 | Sep 10, 2026 | The Health Haven | Every family with grandchildren has two grandmothers. The one the kids run to first. And the other one. And nobody in my family would have hesitated for a second over which one I was. Then one afternoon, buckled into my back seat, my six-year-old granddaughter said eight words that turned me into the other one. And the worst part? When I found out why my family did it — I almost agreed with them. For twelve years, I was the default grandmother. Not the holiday one. The Tuesday one. School pickup three days a week, rain or shine. The after-school hours at my kitchen table. Sleepovers every Friday. I'm the one who knows Nora's cup is the purple one and Sammy's is the green one. And God help you if you get that wrong. I know the pediatrician's number by heart. I know Nora needs the seam of her sock lined up straight or the whole day is ruined. I knew which teacher to hope for before Allison did. Sammy is three. He has fallen asleep on my shoulder every Friday night of his life. That was the whole point of me. Ask anyone. Then, this spring, the pickups went quiet. Brian's hours changed, Allison told me. They had it covered for a while. I should enjoy the break. Two weeks later, the Friday sleepover didn't happen. Sammy had a cold. The Friday after that, Nora had a thing. I believed all of it. I even thought it was sweet — everyone protecting my time like that. Then Allison called and asked a favor. Could I drive Nora home from a birthday party, just this once, because Brian was out of town. Nora buckled herself in, arranged her party bag on her lap, and said, "Grandma Judith does pickup now. She waits by the flagpole." She wasn't being unkind. She's six. She was passing it along the way you'd mention the cafeteria changed the menu. I said, "Does she, sweetheart," and kept my eyes on the road. Two days later, I dropped a dish back at Allison's house. And there it was, on the refrigerator. The new pickup calendar. Tuesday, Wednesday, Friday, printed in Brian's neat engineer handwriting. Judith. Judith. Judith. Nobody had called me. Nobody had sat me down. My name just wasn't on it anymore. I called Allison that evening. "Oh. Mom." A pause I could hear her arranging herself inside. "I was going to call you this week. I promise." Then the voice. My daughter has a voice she uses now that she didn't have two years ago. It sounds like warmth. It lands like a verdict. "We just thought it made more sense for Judith to take the school runs for a while. She's five minutes from the school. It's really about logistics, honestly." I didn't say anything. "We didn't want to make it a whole thing, Mom. That's the only reason I didn't say it straight out." I still didn't say anything. "You've just seemed so tired lately. So worn down. You haven't been yourself since Dad died, and we didn't want to keep asking so much of you." Asking so much of me. Twelve years, and nobody had ever once needed to ask. I waited for the rest of it. There wasn't any rest of it. Just "we'll have you over soon," and the sound of Sammy in the background, and the call was over. Four days later, she called back. "Mom, quick thing — the school forms are due next week and I have no idea what half of these fields even are. You always did them. Could you fill them out and I'll drop them off?" I said of course. "Oh — and Nora's birthday. You know how she is about the details. Nobody plans a party like you do. Would you put it together? The invitations, the cake order, all of it. You're so good at that." I said of course. I hung up and sat at my kitchen table for a long time. And somewhere in that hour, it clicked. They hadn't just taken the pickups. They'd decided — without asking me, without asking my doctor, without asking anyone — that I couldn't be trusted with my own grandchildren. That I'd become something to be managed. But the forms only I understood? The party only I could plan? The cake order, the invitations, the details Nora needs exactly right? Those they still wanted. Because apparently I'm capable enough to run their children's lives from my kitchen table. Just not capable enough to be in them. They didn't want less of me. They wanted my work. They just didn't want me. I filled out the school forms that weekend. Every field, the way I had every August since Nora was in daycare. I planned the party. I ordered the cake from the bakery Nora likes — chocolate inside, white frosting, no exceptions — and addressed sixteen invitations by hand. I dropped the folder at Allison's on a Thursday when I knew nobody would be home, and left it on the porch. I'm not proud of that part. I just couldn't stand in that kitchen and be thanked for it. That evening Allison texted me a photo of the folder on her counter. "MOM. You're a lifesaver. What would we do without you??" I didn't answer that one. And then, the following week, one more call. "Mom — one more thing, and then I promise we'll stop bothering you. Can you set up Deer Lake? You know how the office is with anyone who isn't you." The lake week. Third week of July, the whole family, fourteen summers running. I started it before the grandkids were born. So I called the office and set it up, the way I have every spring — the dates, the deposits, Allison and Brian's cabin, the big one for the cousins, the packing lists for each family. And mine. The small one, by the water. The one that's been mine for fourteen years. Two weeks after the party — a party I planned and attended like a guest — Allison invited me to Sunday dinner. "Just us, Mom. Nothing fancy." I knew the second I walked in. The table was set with the good dishes. Brian was home early. And the kids weren't there. You don't send the kids to Judith's for nothing fancy. We made it through the roast. Brian talked about work. Allison talked about the party — how perfect the cake was, how Nora slept in her party dress. I said the things you say. Then Allison put her fork down. "Mom. We want to talk to you about the lake." My stomach dropped. "We've been talking, and — we think this year it makes sense for you to come up just for the weekend. The middle weekend. Instead of the whole week." I looked at her. "It's my week, Allison. I built that week." "I know, Mom." The voice. "That's not — nobody's saying you didn't." Brian cleared his throat. He'd come with data. "Kathleen, at Easter you dropped the casserole dish and then you sat down on the kitchen floor. Nora saw that. She asked me after if Grandma was okay." "Anyone can drop a dish." "You went to Nora's recital on the wrong Saturday. You sat in an empty auditorium for forty minutes. You told us it was funny." He wasn't being cruel. That was the worst part. He was reading it out like a checklist he'd been keeping for months. "In March you called me Charlie. Twice, in one conversation." I hadn't known that Nora saw the floor. I hadn't known about the name at all. Allison reached across the table and put her hand on mine. "Mom, the lake is a lot. The dock. The stairs down to the water. The kids in and out all day. Last summer you were in bed before Sammy was." I looked at my plate. "And with Dad gone — there's no one in your cabin if something happens at night. We just don't think you should be up there alone for a whole week." She squeezed my hand. "Judith's going to come for the full week this year. She'll help with the kids." There it was. Judith gets my week. I get a weekend. "This comes from love, Mom. You know that, right? You have to understand." You have to understand. They'd watched me since the funeral, collected every dropped dish and every wrong Saturday, and built a case. And the sentence was handed down at the good table, over roast, with the kids safely at the other grandmother's house so they wouldn't hear it. I looked at my daughter. The girl I taught to swim at that lake. "I understand," I said. I picked up my fork and finished my dinner, and I didn't taste one bite of it. There was one thing I hadn't told Allison. One thing I hadn't told anyone. A few weeks before that dinner, I'd had the kids overnight, like always. Sammy fell asleep on my shoulder during the second story, and I carried him out to the porch stairs the way I have a hundred times. On the third step, my chest went tight. Not pain — pressure. Like a hand laid flat on my breastbone, pressing down. The porch light went gray at the edges. I stopped. I couldn't go up. I couldn't turn around. I couldn't put him down. So I stood there, on the third step, holding my sleeping grandson, waiting to find out what my heart was going to do. It let go. The light came back. I climbed the rest of the way with one hand locked on the rail, laid him in his bed, and pressed my shaking hands flat against the mattress until they stopped. He never woke up. I never told a soul. So when my daughter looked at me over the good dishes and said we just don't think you should be up there alone — there was a small voice in me that said: she's right. That's the part I couldn't stand. Not that they'd decided I was finished. That part of me agreed. And I'll tell you what else I never told her. What I never told anyone. I was tired. I'd been tired for two years. Tired in a way sleep didn't touch. Eight hours and I'd wake up like I'd been dragged behind something. My legs ached. Not sore — heavy. A deep, dull ache that lived in my thighs and calves and made my own staircase into something I stood at the bottom of and looked at first. The fog. I'd lose the word for a thing while I was pointing at the thing. I'd walk into a room and stand there. And now I knew — from Brian's checklist, at that table — that I'd called him Charlie twice in March and never even heard myself do it. And underneath all of it, a dread I couldn't put down. Because I knew the reason had a name, and the name was in a drawer in my kitchen, on a lab report, circled in red. High cholesterol. Six weeks after the funeral, I'd gone in for a physical because I could feel my own pulse at night and it scared me. My number came back high. The doctor put me on a statin that same afternoon. Atorvastatin. One small white pill with breakfast. Given my age, he said. Given what had just happened to my husband. It was the responsible thing to do. I took it every morning for fourteen months. I never missed a day. And I got worse. The tiredness got heavier. The fog got thicker. My legs turned to sandbags on the stairs. I felt like I'd aged fifteen years in one. When I told the doctor, he looked at me over his glasses and said it was probably grief. Probably my age. These things take time. And here's the part I couldn't make sense of. The number came down. The doctor showed me the chart at my last visit and said the statin was doing its job. He seemed pleased with me. So the pill was working — on paper. And I was getting worse everywhere except on paper. I didn't have words for that yet. So I did what you do anyway. I bought the fish oil. The red yeast rice. The garlic pills that announced me before I entered a room. The niacin that lit my face on fire for an hour. Oatmeal every morning, whether I wanted it or not. The counter filled up. Nothing changed. Every one of those bottles worked the same way — a flicker of hope, then right back where I was. Everybody had an explanation for me. The doctor said grief. Allison said Dad. Brian had a checklist that said I was simply done. And at three in the morning, lying on my side of a bed that's half empty, I'd do the math. My husband’s heart gave out at 66. Nobody saw it coming. That's what everyone kept saying at the funeral — nobody saw it coming. I'm 64. And something was coming. I could feel it on the porch steps. I'd lie there in the dark, doing that math. That's the woman who booked the cabin. And by the night of that dinner, the lake was ten weeks away. That Sunday, my sister called. Lorraine calls most Sundays. She's four years older than me, lives two hours north — and she is the only person left alive who talks to me like nothing about me has changed. She asked how I was. I said fine. There was a pause, and then she said, "Katie. How are you." And it all came out. The calendar on the refrigerator. The voice Allison uses now. The forms and the party and the good dishes. Brian's checklist. The middle weekend. Judith. I didn't cry until I got to the part about the porch steps. I hadn't planned to tell her that at all. But Lorraine has a way of staying quiet that empties you out, and I heard myself telling her the whole thing — Sammy on my shoulder, the pressure, the gray. When I finished, she was silent for a moment. I expected her to tell me to call a doctor. To tell Allison. To be sensible. Instead she asked me one question. "Katie. The legs. The tiredness. The words. How long has all of that been going on?" "I don't know. A year, more." "And you never said one word of it to me." It wasn't an accusation. It was her doing arithmetic. "That pill they put you on after the funeral. You're still taking it?" "Every morning." "Fourteen months," she said, half to herself. "Katie, I've been describing Dennis for ten minutes." Dennis. Her husband. Four years ago, his doctor put him on a statin — rosuvastatin, a cousin of mine. And Lorraine had watched a man who rewired their whole house by himself turn into someone who napped twice a day and gripped the banister like it owed him money. "The legs," she said. "The fog. Sleeping like the dead and waking up tired. Losing words. Everyone telling him it was his age." "Katie, I sat across from Dennis's doctor while he looked at Dennis's chart and said the numbers were excellent. Excellent. The man couldn't open a jar of pickles, and his chart was excellent." "Dennis is fine now," I said. "I saw him at Christmas. He was up a ladder." "He is now. Because I stopped believing the chart and started reading." "Katie. What if none of this is what they think it is? Not your age. Not your grief. What if it's the pill — and the thing the pill was supposed to fix?" "The pill is working. My number came down. The doctor's pleased with me." "I know," she said. "Dennis's number came down too. That's the part nobody explains. Get a pen." I got a pen. "Your doctor is looking at the wrong thing, Katie," she said. "And so was Dennis's. And so was I, for two years." "What do you mean?" "Cholesterol isn't the problem. I'm not saying it doesn't matter — I'm saying it's not the thing that kills you. Your body makes it on purpose. Your brain runs on it. Your hormones depend on it. It was never the villain." "Then what is?" "When it rusts." I stopped writing. "Say that again." "Rusts. Oxidizes. Same word as the rust on an old fender, same thing that happens to a sliced apple gone brown on the counter. Nobody added anything to the apple. The air did it. Oxidation did it." "And the same thing happens to the cholesterol inside you. Free radicals attack it — stress, the food that comes in boxes, the years — and it goes rancid. It rusts." "And rusted cholesterol turns sticky. It burrows into your artery walls and packs in, layer over layer, year after year, and hardens into plaque." "Then one day a piece of that buildup tears loose, the artery jams shut, and that's the heart attack." "That's the thing that actually kills people, Katie. Not the cholesterol you have. The cholesterol that's gone rancid. The rust." I was quiet. She let me be quiet. "And here's the part nobody explains. The number your doctor watches counts how much cholesterol you've got. It says nothing — nothing — about how much of it has already gone brown. You can have a beautiful number and rusting arteries in the same body." "But my number came down—" "And the rust never stopped. That's the whole trick of it." "The statin goes into your liver and shuts down the production line, so you make less. The number drops. The doctor sees the number drop and says it's working. But it never touches the rust. The cholesterol you still have — and you need it, you can't live without it — keeps rusting, keeps sticking, keeps building. Right where nobody's looking." "That's how a man takes his pill for thirteen years with perfect numbers and still ends up on a table. The chart was never reading the thing that kills you." "It gets worse. When your cholesterol rusts, your body reads that rust as damage — an injury — so it makes more cholesterol to patch it. Which gives the rust more to work on. Which the body reads as more damage. So it makes more still." "It's a wheel. The rust drives you to overproduce, and the more you make, the more there is to rust, and round it goes." "That's the loop the statin can never break. Because the statin only ever chops at the number — the amount. It never touches the rust that's spinning the wheel. It bails water as fast as it can and never once finds the hole the water's coming in through." She paused. And then her voice changed. "Now the part about you. Because there's a second half, and it's the half I watched across my own kitchen table for the better part of two years." "That production line the statin shuts down in your liver? It doesn't only make cholesterol. It also makes something called CoQ10 — the spark every muscle in your body burns to do its work. Your heart, your legs, your hands." "Clamp that line shut to force the number down, and you throttle the spark at the same time. Same switch. You can't shut off one without the other." "The tiredness sleep never touches. The grip going soft. The fog that eats the back half of your own sentences. That's not the cholesterol — high cholesterol has no symptoms at all, it's silent. And it's not your age. And Katie — it is not your grief." "It's the pill, draining the spark out of every muscle you've got. They call it a side effect. It isn't. It's the drug doing exactly what it's built to do." "That's how Dennis's chart said excellent while the man couldn't open a jar. Same pill. Doing both." I sat at my kitchen table with the pen in my hand, and I looked at the list I hadn't known I was making. The legs. The fog. The words. The tiredness. The heart. "Lorraine. The muscle that runs on that spark. The one that would need it most." She was quiet for a second. "The heart, Katie. The heart most of all." The porch steps. Sammy on my shoulder. The pressure, the gray — my heart trying to do its work with the spark half gone, and the rust still building where no chart would ever look. They took my grandchildren away because I was fading. And I was fading because of the pill that was supposed to keep me alive for them. "So the pill fails twice," Lorraine said. "It never stops the rust that's actually killing you. And it drains the spark that keeps you standing." "What Dennis needed — what you need — is the opposite of that. Something that does two things at once. Stops the rust. And leaves the spark alone." "And you found it." "In the last place I expected. It wasn't a drug. It was a pigment." "You know that deep red that stains everything when you cut a beet open? That color has a name. Betalains. It's an antioxidant — but not like any antioxidant you've heard of. It does two things nothing else does." "A beet," I said. "I know how it sounds. I said the same thing to the screen at two in the morning. But hear me out, because this is what took me from reading to believing." "First — most antioxidants are a carpet bomb. They knock out every free radical in you, even the ones your body needs to fight off infection. Betalains are a smart missile. They go after only the exact reaction that turns your cholesterol rancid, and they leave the rest alone." "Second — they actually get in. Carried into the bloodstream, folded right inside the cholesterol particle itself, where the rusting starts." "A statin can't reach in there. Fish oil can't. Nothing on your kitchen counter can."
